Short answer: **the plugin is irrelevant to that question — the build mode decides, and in production the answer is yes, zero branching.**

The mechanics, verified against the source and the built output:

**Production build (what ships):** every HMR site in `Reactive.ts` — there are seven — is gated on `import.meta.env.DEV`, which bundlers replace with the literal `false` at build time. The minifier then dead-code-eliminates the entire arm: no class registry, no construct trap, no grafting code, and no runtime `if` checks left behind, because `if (false && …)` doesn't survive minification. I just re-grepped `dist/index.es.js` and `dist/index.umd.js`: zero occurrences of the HMR machinery. So production runs the pure engine with no branching, whether or not you ever installed `ivueHmr()`.

**Dev server (vite serve):** here's the part worth knowing — `import.meta.env.DEV` is `true` in dev *regardless of the plugin*. So without `ivueHmr()`, the dev runtime still arms its HMR support: the class registry, the construct-trap proxy (the ~11× dev-only instantiation cost), and grafting on module re-execution. What the plugin adds is only the `import.meta.hot.accept()` boundary injection — without it, a class edit still grafts correctly, but the update bubbles to the importing components and remounts them instead of stopping at the class module. If you want production semantics *in dev* (e.g., for benchmarking, as the docs site does), the switch is `globalThis[Symbol.for('ivue.hmr.disable')] = true` before any `Reactive()` call — that kills the construct trap, though the (cheap) `hmrActive()` checks still execute since DEV is statically true there.

So the layering is: **plugin** = update-boundary convenience only; **`ivue.hmr.disable`** = dev-time opt-out of the trap; **build mode** = the thing that actually deletes all branching, unconditionally.

Yes — and it already exists: `globalThis[Symbol.for('ivue.hmr.disable')]` **is** the high-perf dev mode, and it's measured to restore production numbers. The docs site itself runs with it (that's why the in-browser benchmark reports production-equivalent timings on a dev server — we verified that earlier: bare instantiation went from ~11× dev cost back to the prod figure).

What it does and doesn't buy:

- **It kills the construct trap** — the one genuinely expensive piece of dev mode (~11× on bare `new`). That trap exists so post-remount constructions pick up the newest class version; without it, dev construction is production construction.
- **Residual cost is near-zero**: the seven `import.meta.env.DEV && hmrActive()` sites still exist in dev, but `hmrActive()` short-circuits on the disable symbol, and those sites sit on transform/first-access paths, not hot read paths. Reads, method calls, and the ref cache are identical to prod either way.
- **What you lose**: class HMR entirely — edits to `Reactive()` classes will fall back to whatever Vite does normally (component remounts or full reload). Everything else about dev (Vue devtools, Vite HMR for components/CSS) is untouched.

The ergonomic recipe — wire it to an env flag so it's a script, not an edit:

```ts
// main.ts — BEFORE any Reactive() class is constructed
if (import.meta.env.VITE_IVUE_FAST) {
  globalThis[Symbol.for('ivue.hmr.disable')] = true;
}
```

```jsonc
// package.json
"dev":      "vite",
"dev:fast": "VITE_IVUE_FAST=1 vite"
```

So `npm run dev` gives you class HMR, `npm run dev:fast` gives you production-speed instances — switch per terminal session depending on whether today is behavior-editing or perf-feeling work.

If you want this smoother, the natural next step is a `fast` option on the Vite plugin — `ivueHmr({ fast: true })` (or auto-reading the env var) that injects the disable global itself, so apps don't need the `main.ts` line. # Interactive Benchmarks

[ivue vs the World](/guide/model-layer) argues that a domain model —
thousands of live, individually-reactive entities — has a structural memory
cost in idiomatic Vue, and that ivue's laziness erases it. This page is the
receipt: a real, reproducible, end-to-end measurement, not a microbenchmark.
[Performance by Design](/guide/performance) covers the micro-level numbers (creation of
isolated instances, per-read cost); this page covers what happens when you
build an actual grid out of them.

The same 40-column virtualized spreadsheet grid is built three ways from
identical seeded data:

- **Composable** — the idiomatic Vue 3 "composable per entity": every cell

- **ivue** — a `Reactive()` class `$Cell`: `raw` is a ref-getter, three

- **POJO floor** — plain `{ row, col, raw }` objects, no reactivity at all.
  The theoretical memory minimum; edits don't re-render, by design.

# Introducing ivue: plain classes, full reactivity, one kilobyte

Vue's reactivity engine is a general-purpose signals system — and for a
decade, one authoring surface has been missing from it: the plain
TypeScript class. Not a class welded to a component, not a decorator
dialect — an ordinary class, with real inheritance, real encapsulation and
real polymorphism, whose state is fine-grained Vue reactivity.

ivue is that surface. The whole engine is **1.1 kB gzipped**, zero
dependencies, 100% test coverage on every metric.

```ts
import { Reactive } from 'ivue'
import { ref } from 'vue'

class $Counter {
  get count() {
    return ref(0)
  }
  get double() {
    return this.count.value * 2 // plain getter — derives on read
  }
  increment() {
    this.count.value++
  }
}

export const Counter = Reactive($Counter)
```

`Reactive()` transforms the prototype once. A getter returning `ref()`
becomes state — created on first touch, cached, stable forever. A plain
getter stays plain and re-derives on every read, fully reactive with zero
allocation. Methods bind themselves once, to the right `this`. Instances
stay ordinary objects: no proxy wraps them, no work happens at
construction.

Edit a method and the new behavior grafts onto **live instances, state

**Title:** I made plain TypeScript classes fully reactive in Vue 3 — real inheritance, 1.1 kB, and the benchmarks run live in the docs

**Body:**

For the last while I've been building **ivue** — class-based reactivity for Vue 3. Not classes-as-components (that idea deserved to die with `vue-class-component`), but the thing I always actually wanted: an ordinary class as a store, ViewModel, or domain entity, with fine-grained Vue reactivity and zero per-instance cost.

```ts
import { Reactive } from 'ivue'
import { ref } from 'vue'

class $Counter {
  get count() {
    return ref(0)
  }
  get double() {
    return this.count.value * 2 // plain getter — no computed() needed
  }
  increment() {
    this.count.value++
  }
}

export const Counter = Reactive($Counter)
```

`Reactive()` rewrites the prototype once. Ref-returning getters become lazily-cached state. Plain getters stay plain — they re-derive on read, fully reactive through Vue's own dependency tracking, costing **zero bytes per instance** because they live on the prototype. Methods lazy-bind, so `this.method` is always correct and always the same reference — the `() => this.method()` wrapper era ends. Instances are plain objects; no proxy wraps them.

The parts that took the longest weren't the happy path — they were the reasons class reactivity has stayed unsolved: reactive inheritance with `super.x.value` through deep chains, **hot reload that grafts behavior edits onto live instances with state intact**, circular imports resolved structurally by the export pattern, and TypeScript typing ref-getters as writable. All of it works together in 1.1 kB gzipped, zero dependencies, 100% test coverage on every metric.

Numbers (all reproducible, and the benchmarks **run live in the docs** — same shipped engine, in your browser):

- 1,000,000 instances created in **22 ms** (6–132× the alternatives, measured with escape-proof harnesses — the retained-array kind, not the kind V8 optimizes away)
- 100k live observed instances: **3.7 KB each** vs 8–20 KB for composables/`reactive()`, because derivations weigh nothing per instance
- a spreadsheet model with **20,000,000 formula-capable cells at 4.7 bytes/cell** — you can click a button in the docs and build it in your own tab

The honest cost: hot-loop reads go through a getter, several-fold over a raw closure ref. One hoist line (`const width = this.width`) erases it — it's documented with the numbers, not hidden.

Repo: **https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue**

Happy to answer anything — especially skeptical questions, the docs were built to survive them.

parts.text: what's best waay for ppl to install our skill?

The best answer is: **ship the skill inside the npm package, with a one-command installer** — because it gives you the one property no other channel has: *version lock*. The skill is the operating manual for a specific engine; when someone upgrades `ivue`, their agent's instructions should upgrade in the same `npm install`. A skill copied from GitHub main can drift ahead of (or behind) the engine a project actually runs — the exact desync the standard.md mirror discipline exists to prevent, reproduced at the ecosystem level.

Concretely, the tiered design I'd ship:

1. **Primary: `npx ivue skill`** — a tiny `bin` in the package that copies `node_modules/ivue/skills/ivue/SKILL.md` into the project's `.claude/skills/ivue/`. One command, no network beyond the install they already did, always matching their installed version. (~30 lines: resolve own package dir, `mkdir -p`, copy, print "installed — matches ivue vX.Y.Z"; refuse to overwrite local modifications unless `--force`.) The same command can later grow targets: `npx ivue skill --cursor` writing `.cursorrules`-style output for non-Claude agents, since the manual is plain markdown.

2. **Fallback for the curious / non-users:** the one-liner without installing anything —
   `npx degit infinite-system/ivue/.claude/skills/ivue .claude/skills/ivue`
   Good for evaluating the skill before adopting the library; documented as the "try it" path with the caveat that it tracks main, not their version.

3. **The docs page stays the human channel.** The Standard page already links the raw file; add a small "Install as a skill" info box at its top showing command #1 — the page is where people discover the skill exists, so the install affordance belongs there, plus a line in Getting Started next to the `ivueHmr` setup and one in the README's "Built for humans and AI" section.

What I'd *not* do: a separate `ivue-skill` npm package (second thing to version-sync — recreates the drift problem), or leading with a Claude-plugin marketplace listing (Claude-specific, more moving parts; fine as a later addition, wrong as the primary path since `.claude/skills/` in-repo already works natively and travels with the codebase through git, which means one teammate installing it equips the whole team).

# Your objects are rented from the framework

![Your objects are rented from the framework](/blog/rented-objects.png)

Here is a test you can run on any Vue codebase in thirty seconds: find the
order, the invoice, the document — the *thing* your product is actually
about — and ask where it lives. In most codebases the answer is: nowhere.
It exists as fragments — a composable here, a pinia slice there, props
threaded four levels down — and every fragment's lifetime is chained to
whatever component happens to be mounted. Close the tab panel, and your
"order" ceases to exist.

That's not architecture. That's renting.

A domain object deserves what every object in every other kind of software
has had for fifty years: **identity, state, behavior, and a lifetime it
owns**. The reason frontend gave that up isn't philosophical — it's that
making a class reactive used to cost too much: a proxy per object, eager
computeds per field, `this` breaking in every handler. So the field
normalized statelessness and called it a virtue.

ivue re-prices the deal. An instance is a plain object; nothing allocates
until first access; derivations live once, on the prototype. The measured
consequence: **one million live class instances in 22 ms and 3.7 KB each
under observation** — populations that OOM every alternative pattern on
the same machine. At that price, your order can simply *be an object*
again — watchable, derivable, inheritable — constructed where you choose,
disposed when you say:

```ts
class $Order {
  get items() {
    return shallowRef<OrderItem[]>([]);
  }


… [18,133 characters removed from the sample] …

own harnesses hid.
date: 2026-07

# Measured, not promised

![Measured, not promised](/blog/measured-not-promised.png)

Every library's benchmarks are flattering. Not because authors lie —
because **benchmarks lie by default**, and it takes real work to stop
them. Building ivue's numbers, our own harnesses lied to us three times.
This post is the confession log, because the failure modes live in your
benchmarks too.

**Lie one: the JIT deleted the competition.** Our first creation
benchmark wrote instances into one overwritten variable. V8's escape
analysis elided the competitors' allocations entirely — `reactive()`
"created" 100,000 proxies in 0.0 ms — while ivue's opaque construction
kept honestly paying. The fix: every instance retained in an array,
touched after timing. Nothing the optimizer can discard.

**Lie two: the unobserved heap.** Our first memory benchmark read
instances *outside any effect* — and `reactive()` looked impossibly
light, because a proxy allocates its dependency storage only when
something subscribes. Live objects are *observed* objects. Re-measured
with every instance read inside its own subscribing effect, the proxy's
real bill arrived: dependency maps for every tracked key.

**Lie three: the harness tax.** Timing operations through a per-call
closure added a constant cost to every variant — large enough to hide a
3× difference between two method-call styles. Loop inside the timed
region, or measure the harness instead of the code.

What survived the discipline ships on the [Performance by
Design](/guide/performance) page with its protocol attached — and the
sharpest habit we kept: **run the numbers in the reader's browser**, on
the shipped engine, where no one can quietly pick the machine:

<DemoPerf />

If a claim can't survive its own methodology section, it isn't a result —
it's marketing with axes. Steal the harness patterns; they're described
under [Methodology](/guide/benchmarks#methodology).

  V8 elide the work — `reactive()` showed 0.0ms. Escape-proof protocol: push
  every instance into a retained array + do a liveness read pass after timing.
- **"At rest" heap flatters proxies.** Reading state OUTSIDE an effect made
  `reactive()` look smaller than ivue — its dependency storage only allocates
  when the first observer subscribes. Correct protocol: **observed heap** —
  read every property inside a per-instance subscribing effect, then measure.
  (User's instinct "reactive() can't be smaller than ivue" was right.)
- **Per-op closure harness tax hides real differences.** Calling the measured
  op through a fresh closure per iteration added ~uniform overhead that masked
  a 3× gap (dotted method ~4ns vs hoisted ~1.4ns). Correct protocol: put the
  loop INSIDE the timed region.
- Heap table final protocol: 100k instances (1M OOMs), 10 refs + 30 derivations.
  Results: ivue 3.7KB/instance, closures 2.1×, reactive() 2.8×, computeds 5.3×.

# LESSONS.md — hard-won lessons that must not perish

Append-only knowledge base for humans and AI agents working on this repo.
When a session learns something the hard way (a broken build, a wrong
published number, a shell trap), it gets a bullet here — with the failure
that taught it. Read this before touching benchmarks, docs, or releases.

## Benchmarking — the escape-proof protocol

Three published tables were wrong before these rules existed. Every wrong
number was a **harness artifact, not library behavior** — when a number
"seems wrong", suspect the harness first.

- **Retain what you create.** Instances created but never read get elided by
  the JIT — `reactive()` once showed 0.0ms for 100k creations. Push every
  instance into a retained array and do a liveness read pass after timing.
- **Measure heap _observed_, not at rest.** Reading state outside an effect
  flatters proxies: `reactive()`'s dependency storage only allocates when the
  first observer subscribes, so at-rest it looks smaller than ivue — which is
  impossible in real apps. Protocol: read every property inside a
  per-instance subscribing effect, then snapshot heap.
- **Loop inside the timed region.** Calling the measured op through a fresh
  per-iteration closure adds uniform overhead that masks real gaps — it hid a
  3× difference (dotted method ~4ns vs hoisted ~1.4ns).
- Heap standard: **100k instances** (1M OOMs the VM), 10 refs + 30 derivations.
- Published numbers always carry method + environment. Never publish a number
  not re-run under this protocol.

## VitePress (docs_v2) traps

- The markdown-it base-prefix pass must rewrite **`href` only, never `src`** —
  VitePress resolves image `src` (public dir + base) itself; prefixing src
  breaks the Rollup build ("failed to resolve /ivue/...png").
- Frontmatter values starting with `"` or a backtick break YAML — single-quote
  or rephrase.
- Literal `{{ }}` in prose SSR-compiles as interpolation — rephrase or `v-pre`.
- Scope wide CSS to `.VPDoc`: `.benchmarks-wide .content` once matched the
  navbar's `.content` and broke it.
- Dead in-page anchors do NOT fail the build — check linked anchors in built HTML.
- Code-block scrolling: the `div[class*='language-']` wrapper owns
  `max-height` + `overflow-y: auto`; the inner `pre` must stay
  `overflow-y: visible` — otherwise double scrollbars and desynced line numbers.
- After ANY docs change: `npm run build:docs` must pass before claiming done.

## Shell / environment (Parallels Linux VM, shared macOS node_modules)

- **Never rebuild native binaries / `npm ci`** — node_modules is shared with
  the macOS host; rebuilding breaks the other side.
- `pkill -f 'vite demo'` matches and kills its own invocation (exit 144) —
  always bracket the pattern: `pkill -f '[v]ite demo'`.
- Foreground `sleep` is blocked in the agent sandbox (exit 144), and
  `curl --retry-delay` sleeps too — run waiting commands in the background.
- **Backticks inside `git commit -m "..."` execute as commands** (yields
  `ivue: command not found` + a truncated message). Single-quote messages.
- `echo 'x' >> file` glues onto the last line when the file lacks a trailing
  newline — check before appending (this once corrupted .gitignore).
- Docs dev server runs at `localhost:5174/ivue/` — the `/ivue/` base matters.

## Library / packaging

- **The exports map is a release gate.** `ivue/hmr-plugin` was once
  unresolvable (only `"."` exported) AND shipped as raw TS that node can't
  load from a vite.config. Subpaths must be compiled (`dist/*.mjs` + `.d.ts`)
  and exported. Test `import('ivue/subpath')` from a packed tarball
  (`npm pack`) before publishing.
- `import.meta.env.DEV` must stay a static **dotted** read so production DCE
  works; `import.meta.env['TEST']` must stay a **bracket** read — vitest
  statically inlines the dotted form and creates untestable phantom branches.
- v8 coverage quirks: `??` remaps to phantom branches (prefer statement-level
  `if`); the test transform strips comments, so source-scanner comment paths
  are only reachable via `new Function` raw sources.
- String processing on user source (hmrNormalize): a state-tracking scanner
  beats regex — the regex version collapsed whitespace **inside string
  literals**, silently corrupting semantics.
- Production size gate: the engine is ~1.1 KB gzipped — re-verify the build
  size after any engine edit; DCE regressions are silent.

## Docs writing (full rules: `.claude/skills/write-docs/SKILL.md`)

- Timeless present — never contrast against a draft state the reader never
  saw ("it is Y, not X" where X never shipped).
- Never reference by number ("Principle #4") — numbering changes; link by name.
- One name per concept everywhere (it's an "invariant", never law/rule/principle).
- Every code block follows the ivue skill; blocks with a filename comment are
  full-canon templates; class files are PascalCase.
- Live demos import the SAME files the page shows as code blocks.
- The ivue skill file is the source; `docs_v2/guide/standard.md` is a spliced
  mirror — never edit the mirror directly.
- Theme styles every guide blockquote as an invariant card — reserve `>` for
  statements that deserve it.

## Big lists (the 1M-row scroller)

- A million items stay memory-sane by sharing ~24 body-string variants and
  rendering the row number from a `position` field — unique strings per row
  cost hundreds of MB. Measured result: 12 DOM rows, ~201 MB total page heap.

## Process

- **Verify before claiming**: browser-drive every live embed, screenshot both
  themes for design changes, run a 375px horizontal-overflow check after
  layout changes.
- CLI `--all`-style flags detect-and-equip existing tool footprints; they
  never scaffold vendor folders the project doesn't use (see `bin/ivue.mjs`).
